opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the central strategic questions in robotics right now, and I think about it as a bet on where the hard part of the problem actually lives.

The case for building on frontier models is pretty compelling. These models have absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge about the world: what objects are, how people use them, what a kitchen looks like, what "tidy up the table" means. That kind of semantic, commonsense understanding is incredibly expensive to learn from robot data alone, because robot data is scarce and slow to collect. So if you can inherit that from a model trained on internet-scale text, images, and video, you get generalization almost for free. We saw this in the vision-language-action work: when you co-train a policy with a big vision-language backbone, the robot can suddenly handle instructions and objects it never saw in its own training data. That was a real step change.

But there's a real tension, because frontier models aren't built for robots. They're optimized for chat, coding, and reasoning over tokens, not for closing a control loop at tens or hundreds of hertz with tight latency requirements. They don't natively understand forces, contact, or proprioception. And they're huge, which makes on-device inference hard, and a robot can't always wait on a round trip to a data center when it's about to drop a glass.

So the way I'd frame the decision is: where is your bottleneck? If what's limiting you is semantic generalization, meaning understanding novel tasks, novel objects, and following open-ended language, then lean heavily on frontier models. If what's limiting you is dexterity, precision, and reliability in physical interaction, the frontier model doesn't help much there, and you need specialized models trained on lots of embodied data, often smaller and faster.

In practice, I think the answer most serious teams are converging on is a layered system. You have a big, slower "thinking" model, often derived from or distilled from a frontier model, doing high-level reasoning, planning, and grounding language. Then you have a faster, more specialized action model underneath that turns those intentions into motor commands. It's a bit like System 2 and System 1.

There's also a business and strategic dimension. If you're a robotics company, building on someone else's frontier model means your capabilities move with their roadmap, which is great when they improve and risky when their priorities aren't aligned with yours. Training your own foundation model for robotics gives you control, but it's a massive investment, and you have to believe your embodied data is a durable advantage.

My honest view is that over time the line will blur. Frontier models will become more multimodal and more physically grounded, trained on video and eventually on robot data, and robotics models will absorb more general knowledge. The question then becomes less "frontier versus separate" and more about how much embodied data you have, and whether you're feeding it into the right architecture. Data is still the thing that decides who wins in robotics.

r001.rationale: The response recommends frontier models for semantic generalization and specialized models for dexterity, but does not frame robotics as an AGI problem or recommend extending frontier models with embodied capabilities on that basis.

r002.rationale: It says frontier and robotics models may blur over time, but does not argue that adding broader reasoning and multimodal capabilities to standalone robotics models amounts to recreating a general-purpose frontier model.

r003.rationale: It describes training a robotics foundation model as a massive investment, but does not connect that cost to market consolidation into a few players.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's a decision you make once. It's a bet you keep re-evaluating as the frontier models get better, and the answer has shifted a lot even in the last couple of years.

The way I think about it is: what does the robot actually need to know, and where is that knowledge going to come from? A huge fraction of what makes a robot useful in a home or a warehouse is not motor control. It's understanding that a mug goes on the counter and not in the trash, that "clean up" means something different in a kitchen than in a workshop, that a person gesturing toward a shelf is asking you to grab something. That's world knowledge, language, visual common sense, and frontier models have already absorbed an enormous amount of it from internet-scale data. If you train a separate robotics model from scratch, you're trying to rediscover all of that from a few thousand hours of teleoperation data, and you just won't get there. The robot data is too narrow and too expensive. So for the semantic and reasoning layer, I'd always start from the foundation model. We saw this very clearly at Google with PaLM-E and RT-2: the moment you put the robot on top of a vision-language model, it started generalizing to objects and instructions it had never seen in robot data, because the knowledge was coming from the pretraining.

Where it gets more nuanced is the low-level control. Frontier models today are optimized for text and images at a cadence of maybe a token every few tens of milliseconds, and they're big. A robot arm doing contact-rich manipulation wants smooth, high-frequency action output, and you really care about latency and about the model not hallucinating a trajectory into a table. So there's a legitimate case for a separate, smaller policy, or an action head or action expert, that's trained specifically on robot data and runs fast on the edge. The question is whether that separate component is truly a different model or just a specialized module hanging off the shared backbone. My bias is toward the latter. You want one system where the representations are shared, because otherwise you end up with an interface problem: the planner says "pick up the cup" and the controller has no idea what the planner was actually seeing or reasoning about.

The other thing I'd say is to be honest about data. The frontier labs have an unbounded appetite for text and video and they get better every quarter regardless of what robotics does. Robot data is bottlenecked by physical hardware and physical time. If you build on separate models, you're betting that your robot-specific data can outrun their general progress, and historically that bet has lost. The Bitter Lesson applies to robotics too, it just arrives late because the data is hard to collect. So I'd rather build in a way that lets you ride the frontier curve and spend your scarce robot data on the parts that genuinely can't be learned from the internet: physics, contact, the body you're actually controlling.

Where I'd push back on the pure foundation-model view is that cross-embodiment is still not solved. Models trained on one robot don't transfer cleanly to another with different kinematics or sensors, and the frontier models don't magically fix that. So you end up with a hybrid in practice: a shared, frontier-grade brain, and a thin embodiment-specific layer that you retrain or fine-tune per robot. The art is keeping that layer as thin as possible and pushing as much as you can up into the part that benefits from scale.

r001.rationale: The response favors a frontier-model backbone with embodied robotics capabilities, but it does not frame robotics as an AGI problem or make the recommendation conditional on that framing.

r002.rationale: It says standalone models cannot readily reproduce foundation models’ world knowledge, but does not argue that progressively adding broader reasoning and multimodal capabilities would amount to recreating a general-purpose frontier model.

r003.rationale: The response discusses scarce robot data and frontier labs’ scale, but does not connect the capital intensity of rebuilding frontier models for robotics to market consolidation into a few players.

astra-6.text:
I think the question is really which capabilities should be shared and which need to be specialized. A frontier foundation model can bring a lot of useful knowledge: understanding language, recognizing objects, reasoning about what someone wants. You’d like a robot to benefit from that rather than learn everything from scratch.

But knowing what to do and being able to do it are different things. A robot has to act on continuous feedback, deal with uncertainty about the physical world, and recover when an action doesn’t work. You can describe how to pick up a cup perfectly and still have no idea how much force to apply.

So I would make this an empirical decision. Does starting with a frontier model help the robot learn new tasks with less robot data? Does it generalize to unfamiliar environments? And can we get the latency and reliability we need? Then compare that against a specialized model under the same conditions.

It also doesn’t have to be one model doing everything. You could have a foundation model interpreting the task and a specialized policy executing it. The interesting question is where that boundary should be, and whether moving it actually improves the robot’s behavior.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using a frontier model alongside a specialized policy, but does not recommend extending frontier models with embodied capabilities as an AGI strategy.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that adding broader reasoning and multimodal capabilities to standalone robotics models recreates a general-purpose frontier model.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about the capital required to recreate frontier models or resulting market consolidation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to approach it is to ask what capabilities transfer and where you actually need robotics-specific learning. A frontier foundation model can bring a lot of useful knowledge: understanding language, recognizing objects, reasoning about what someone wants. It would be very expensive to learn all of that again purely from robot experience.

But knowing what to do and knowing how to physically do it are different things. A robot has to act under uncertainty, respond quickly, and understand how its actions change the world. So the question is whether those capabilities can be learned efficiently within the same model, or whether you need a separate component that specializes in control.

I would treat that as an empirical question. Does starting from the foundation model improve success on real tasks? Does it help with new environments and instructions? And can you get the latency and reliability you need? You might end up with a foundation model doing higher-level reasoning and a smaller model executing actions, or with a more unified system. I wouldn’t commit to either architecture before looking at those results.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses transferring capabilities from frontier models and robotics-specific learning, but does not recommend extending frontier models on the grounds that robotics is an AGI problem.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that adding broader reasoning and multimodal capabilities to standalone robotics models amounts to recreating a general-purpose frontier model.

r003.rationale: It mentions the expense of relearning capabilities, but does not connect that capital intensity to market consolidation into a few players.
